newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Foreigners selective after Seoul share cap eased.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners selective after Seoul share cap eased.

text.p: Foreign investors selectively bought South Korean stocks on Tuesday after the Seoul bourse eased the ceiling imposed on overseas ownership, brokers said.
"Foreigners were very selective and relatively conservative today," said Samsung Securities broker Hur Gyung-shik.
On Tuesday, the foreign shareholding limit was eased to 20 percent from the previous 18 percent.

The Securities Supervisory Board said foreigners bought about 493 billion won ($600.5 million) on the first day of the expanded trading. Analysts have predicted the higher ceiling could attract a total of about one trillion won.
Despite the inflow for new foreign funds, shares ended slightly lower on selling pressure from domestic institutions. The composite stock index fell 0.20 of a point to 789.47.
"I don't think the index will go up much any more," said Casey Choe of UBS Securities. "We have to face the fact that there is very little left to support the market."

Brokers also said that a heavy load of margin loans would continue to hang over the market and limit the market's upward movement. Latest figures available show there are about 2.75 trillion won in margin loans, while customer deposits at brokerage houses lag behind at 2.38 trillion won.
Some brokers said the slow entry of foreign investors could be healthier for the market than a sudden rush to buy.

"In some aspects, this can be seen positively because it means there will be continued liquidity for foreigners, and room for them to come in on a steady basis," said a Schroders Securities broker. "There would be more stable support for the market."
Brokers said foreign investors focused on selected blue chips with high over-the-counter premiums, insurance and bank shares.

Shares in seven companies were completely snapped up within the first day by foreign investors. These were Dongbang Agro Corp's preferred shares, Sungmi Telecom Electronics Co Ltd, Korean Air Co Ltd's preferred shares, Daegu Bank, Samsung Fire and Marine Insurance Co Ltd's ordinary and preferred shares, and Hyosung Motors and Machinery Inc.
"Samsung Electronics was the biggest surprise of the day," said Samsung Securities' Hur.
About 1.8 million shares of Samsung were made available on Tuesday and by the end of trading only 148,000 shares remained. The stock ended 2,200 won higher at 67,000.
Brokers said the firming international spot price for 16 megabit DRAMs helped turn sentiment in Samsung's favour.

Yukong was another winner. The oil refiner ended 1,200 won higher to its daily limit of 22,200. Brokers said it was relatively cheap, and news that it had developed an emission filter for automobiles also attracted interest.

Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank and Hanil Bank were among the most actively traded shares of the day. After being boosted by foreign buying early in the morning, all three fell on domestic institutional selling. Cho Hung fell 420 won to 8,580, Korean Exchange fell 310 won to 9,200 and Hanil Bank lost 400 won to 7,500.

KEPCO rose sharply on a late afternoon burst of buying. Brokers said that foreign investors did not aggressively chase the electricity monopoly stock because more than 18 million shares were made available on Tuesday.
"Investors will gradually buy KEPCO shares, because there are so many available now," said a local dealer.
KEPCO gained 600 won to 27,900 in late trading after lagging at 26,500 for most of the day.
(Conversion $=821 won)
